extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors, pro se patent applicants, small business owners, and entrepreneurs seeking to perform prior art patent searches
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory guidance on how to plan and perform a complete prior art patent search (text, classification, and citation searching), how to identify prior art sources, and where to find patent search resources (USPTO and foreign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Realize the need for a Prior Art Search
rubrics_metrics.description: At the conclusion of this presentation participants will be able to: Realize the need for a Prior Art Search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the landscape of the field of invention to identify opportunities for innovation, competitors in the field, and sharpen your invention to differentiate from competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether the invention already exists / avoid public disclosure before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: According to U.S. patent law, an invention cannot be patented if the claimed invention was described in a printed publication, on sale, available to the public, or in public use before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain confidentiality — do not publicly disclose, offer for sale, or otherwise make the invention public prior to filing, because such disclosures can be prior art that bars patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Information known publicly before the effective filing date of a U.S. patent application is called prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art consists of information available to the public before the effective filing date and includes U.S. patents and published patent applications, foreign patents and published patent applications, journal & magazine articles, books, manuals, catalogs, websites, conference proceedings, and scientific papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize formats and modern sources of prior art (websites, social media, electronic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may be published on paper or electronic format; websites, social media, and various other forms of online publications are frequently cited as valid sources of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only traditional publications count — include web pages, social posts, videos, and other electronic publications (use archive.org/Wayback Machine for historical captures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all three types of patent research for a complete search
rubrics_metrics.description: Three major types of prior art patent searches: Text searching, Patent classification searching, and Patent citation searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete patent search will involve all three methods; rely on their complementary strengths rather than only one approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text searching: identify concepts and perform multi-database searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify main concepts of the invention, develop words and terms for each concept, and perform text research using multiple databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple web and patent databases to run text searches on the vocabulary you derive; don't depend on a single database or single term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify main concepts by repeated single-sentence descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the invention in a single written sentence. Perform the same exercise a minimum of three (3) times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the three sentences and review words/terms that appear frequently — repetition often indicates a major concept. Example sentences given for a 'camping bicycle' help extract keywords like folding frame, portable, backpack, detachable wheels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand vocabulary using dictionaries, manuals, and technical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dictionaries, technical manuals, and the internet to discover additional words and terms for concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect synonyms and alternative terms (e.g., Backpack or Rucksack or Knapsack; Bicycle or 'Two Wheeled Vehicle'; Folding or Hinged or Collapsible) to broaden text search coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad-to-narrow searching strategy (select a primary concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by identifying main concepts and selecting a primary concept — the single concept that all search results must have in order to be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the primary concept (X1) as a filter, add other concepts in order of priority (X2–Xn), and iteratively narrow results. Pause when a result set is small enough to review. When conducted correctly, this strategy helps ensure the primary concept is present in final results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification searching: use classification codes to focus searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classification codes to search for prior art, determine the relevant technical area, and limit or focus the search to a specific area of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching by classification can find relevant patents that use different vocabulary than your text searches; use it to target specific technology areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPC is a harmonized classification scheme (USPTO + EPO) divided into main areas (A–H) and hierarchical subclasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the CPC to find appropriate classes for your invention (examples: B62K 3/00 Land vehicles, bicycles; B62K 15/00 Collapsible or foldable cycles; A45F3/00, A45F4/00). The CPC helps narrow searches to relevant subclasses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and search the CPC scheme via USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic version of the CPC classification scheme is available online through the USPTO website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Navigate to www.uspto.gov and access the electronic CPC scheme (e.g., search for 'cpc scheme' + terms) to discover candidate classes for your invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean and combination classification searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Boolean classification search techniques to combine classes and concepts when searching classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine classification codes and search terms logically to refine results (slides reference 'Boolean classification search' and sample results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent citation searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use patent citation searching as one of the major search methods (searching by references cited and citing patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow backward citations (references cited) and forward citations (later patents citing a patent) to expand or trace relevant patent families and related art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use USPTO search tools and know their purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO resources include Examiner’s Automated Search Tool (PubEAST), Web-based Examiner Search Tool (PubWEST), PatFT, AppFT, PAIR, Patent Assignment Database, and Global Dossier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know each tool’s scope: PubEAST & PubWEST (tools used by examiners; public access only at USPTO offices and PTRCs), PatFT (full-text patents 1976–present; PDF images back to 1790), AppFT (published patent applications), PAIR (prosecution history), Global Dossier (family search and examination results), Assignment Database (ownership records). Use the tools appropriate to the search task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand access limitations and coverage of USPTO databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some USPTO examiner tools (PubEAST, PubWEST) are available only at USPTO offices and Patent and Trademark Resource Centers (PTRCs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publicly available tools (PatFT, AppFT, Global Dossier, Assignment DB) for remote searching; visit PTRCs or USPTO offices if you need examiner-only resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non‑USPTO and supplementary databases (Google Patents, archive.org, technical journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement USPTO searches with Google Patent Search, general web search engines, archive.org/Wayback Machine, video websites, IEEE databases, scientific journals, magazines, and newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include non-patent literature and archived web captures when searching for prior art; video and web content can be relevant prior art and may require use of archival tools to verify historical availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use foreign patent office resources and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Search foreign patent databases and translation services (EPO Espacenet, JPO, KIPO, WIPO PATENTSCOPE) to find non-U.S. documents and use machine translations where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign databases often provide machine translations and large document collections (e.g., Espacenet single-line search, PATENTSCOPE covering millions of documents). Use them to locate international prior art and family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative refinement and manageability of result sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Iteratively refine searches (broad to narrow) and pause when a set of results is small enough to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat searching as iterative: refine concepts, add/remove terms and classifications, and stop to analyze promising results before continuing refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep confidentiality and seek help when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidentiality is important; the USPTO provides assistance to independent inventors via the Pro Se Assistance Center and Patent and Trademark Resource Centers (PTRCs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use USPTO help resources (Pro Se Assistance Center, Inventors Assistance Center, Patents Ombudsman, Application Assistance Unit, PTRCs) for guidance on searches, forms, and filing. Pro Se Assistance contact info and hours provided (webpage, email, phone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patent assignment and prosecution histories to understand ownership and file histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Assignment Database and PAIR provide assignment records and prosecution histories, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check assignment records to learn ownership changes and use PAIR to review file wrappers and examination history to assess scope and prosecution-related prior art or rejections.
